Good afternoon, everyone, colleagues.
Ahla wa sahla.

And thank you for joining us this afternoon for this important Area Formula meeting on transitional justice and missing persons in the Syrian Arab Republic. I would also like to welcome our co-sponsors, Colombia, Luxembourg, and the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as our 4 distinguished briefers. Your collective commitment to this issue both here at the United Nations and on the ground in Syria, is highly commendable. We particularly wish to acknowledge the recent historical steps taken by Syria in this regard, as well as the important work of Syrian survivors and civil society. We look forward to hearing your insights. Colleagues, throughout nearly 14 years of civil war, more than half a million Syrians were killed, and hundreds of thousands of Syrian civilians are estimated to have disappeared. For millions of Syrians, it seemed as though the fate of their loved ones would remain unknown and that justice would forever remain out of reach. However, since the fall of the Assad regime, and thanks to the commitment of Syria to the transitional justice process, there is now a real possibility to make progress, to support justice and accountability for the Syrian people, in line with international standards, and to restore dignity for survivors who have suffered for too long. Addressing this legacy— the legacy of these violations through a comprehensive, transparent, and inclusive transitional justice process is essential. Such a process can help rebuild trust in national institutions, end the culture of impunity, and help to ensure that Syria does not slide back into conflict. But Syria is not alone in these efforts. In Resolution 2282, the Security Council recognized transitional justice as integral to sustaining peace, making this track a matter of continuing importance for us here and for the international community. The Security Council and the broader UN membership can support a range of technical efforts, enabling international justice mechanisms to share more information with relevant Syrian bodies, support relevant Syrian institutions in their efforts to lead the transitional justice process, and backing a holistic, coordinated approach that improves the chances of uncovering the truth and bringing perpetrators to justice. But we can also ensure sustained political support— support for the efforts of Syria with the full involvement of civil society, including women and youth, and grounded in in human rights. We hope that today's meeting can address these important discussions. Colleagues, 15 years ago, in 2011, I was Denmark's Ambassador to Syria and met frequently with peaceful opposition figures and human rights defenders during the Syrian uprising. One person made a particular impression on me, a young woman human rights lawyer and civil society activist, Rassane Seytouni. We met at her secret location where she had gone into hiding from the regime. And she was one of the most fearless and impressive people I ever met. In December 2013, she was kidnapped together with her husband and 2 other activists, and she has been missing ever since. So for me, this meeting is for her, her family and friends, and all the other Syrians who have suffered so much not knowing the whereabouts of their loved ones. And with that, I now pass the floor to my colleague, Ambassador Salabarte Torres of Colombia.

Excellencies, Colombia is delighted to co-sponsor this meeting together with Denmark, Luxembourg, and Syria, and we are grateful for the participation of our distinguished briefers and all of the delegations joining us. We are here to discuss a topic which is essential for the efforts that is being undertaken by Syria to address the legacy of the grave violations of the past and to guarantee that the victims play a central role in the quest for truth, justice, reparation, and non-repetition. At the same time, looking at how to make progress in shedding light on the whereabouts of the missing persons as part of building a sustainable and lasting peace in the country. In this context, transitional justice represents a fundamental element. Its purpose isn't solely to clarify responsibilities for the grave violations of the past, but also to recognize the dignity of the victims, to guarantee their rights, and to contribute to rebuilding the social fabric and towards social reconciliation. All of these efforts represent an opportunity to strengthen the rule of law as well. The situation of missing persons is a priority in all of this work. Behind every missing person, there are families that continue to live amidst uncertainty uncertainty and communities that are still waiting for answers. Shedding light on their fate and whereabouts is a humanitarian imperative and part and parcel of restoring trust among the public in their institutions. Our own experience in Colombia has taught us that victims, their families, and civil society organizations are not solely the beneficiaries of transitional justice processes. They are crucial stakeholders in the design, legitimacy, and implementation of these processes. Their effective involvement strengthens institutions and contributes to building a more robust and inclusive peace. And in this regard, we'd like to highlight the fundamental role played by women seekers of missing persons. Many cases have shed light on the whereabouts of missing persons, preserved memory, documented the truth, and also highlighted the importance of truth and justice. Justice, very often facing risks for their own security. In this regard, we are pleased to say that together with the Syrian Arab Republic, we will be putting forward a proposal to the General Assembly to recognize this role. Our experience has reaffirmed the truth of this reality, and it has brought our country to recognize the role of women who look for missing persons as proponents of peace, as well as to promote their effective involvement in processes related to the quest for truth and memory. We believe that this recognition reflects a universal principle. Those who dedicate their lives to looking for missing persons should be able to enjoy the necessary guarantees to carry out this work safely, with dignity, and with full respect for their rights. Excellencies, Colombia believes that it is fundamental that Syrian authorities are able to enjoy the support and accompaniment of the United Nations and international mechanisms relevant in this area, including the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic, the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism, and the U.N. Independent Commission of Inquiry, always as a part of a Syrian-led process based on the needs and priorities defined by Syrians themselves. Finally, I would like to underscore that the quest for missing persons transcends political divisions. It is above all a humanitarian obligation and an expression of respect for human dignity. Placing victims and their families in the spotlight of this effort doesn't only contribute to shedding light on the truth, it also contributes to guaranteeing reconciliation and moving towards peace. Thank you very much. Gracias.

I thank Ambassador Salabata for her statement, and I now pass the floor to Ambassador Olivier Maes, Permanent Representative of Luxembourg to the United Nations.

You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Ambassador Lassen. Dear Christina, colleagues, distinguished guests, and dear families of the missing joining us today, it is an honour for Luxembourg to co-sponsor this Area Formula meeting together with Denmark, Colombia, and the Syrian Arab Republic. Dear Christina, you reminded us that hundreds of thousands of people went missing during the Assad regime, and the fate of a vast majority of those remains unknown. This creates incredible hardship for those left behind, both in Syria and abroad. In an effort to bring closure to the families and to clarify the fate of the missing, in June 2023, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 77301, by which it decided to establish, under the auspices of these United Nations, the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic. Luxembourg was honored then to lead the core group of member states that worked hard to establish the IIMP under very challenging circumstances 3 years ago. Throughout our joint work on Resolution 77301, we have always put the dignity of the missing and the well-being of their families at the forefront of our efforts. The families were the real driving force behind the creation of the institution, and we are very heartened to see that they remain engaged and that their perspectives are included in the work of the institution, and I'm particularly moved to see representatives of Syrian families, very courageous Syrian women present with us today in this room. Since the fall of the Assad regime and the establishment of the Syrian Transitional Authorities, new pathways have opened to clarify the fate of the missing. The fact that the head of the IIMP, Assistant Secretary-General Carla Quintana, and her team have been able to conduct numerous working visits to Syria has been crucial for the progress of the work of the institution, and we hope that the cooperation will grow stronger in the future. We are encouraged by the ongoing national efforts and welcome the participation of the heads of the Syrian National Commission for the Missing and the Syrian National Commission on Transitional Justice in today's meeting. The process of clarifying the fate of the missing indeed needs to be Syrian-owned, nationally-led, and internationally supported. We very much hope that today's meeting will help strengthen the cooperation and the trust between all relevant actors in Syria and in the international community to ensure the right of families to know the fate and whereabouts of their missing relatives and to receive adequate support. It is a humanitarian imperative. It is also an imperative for peace, because addressing the issue of missing persons is crucial in the efforts towards national reconciliation and sustainable peace in Syria. Thank you very much.
And I thank Ambassador Mass for his statement, and I now pass the floor to Ambassador Ibrahim Olavi. Permanent Representative of Syria to the United Nations. Tafaddal.

Thank you, colleagues. I thank my esteemed colleagues, the Friends of the Syrian People, the Ambassadors of Denmark, Luxembourg, and Colombia, and to all of you, those with us here today, for joining us and for co-sponsoring this event. Before the lunch break, I had pre-prepared remarks, And during lunch— but during the lunch break, I had a conversation with both Yasmin and Safinaz, the 2 brave women you see sitting behind me. This is not the first time they hear of the United Nations, nor the first time some of them enter it, but it's the first time that they're sitting here together with Syria and with states, being able to talk about something that we actually can do something about. I want to go back to December 7th, not 8th. On December 7th, towards— while we can see Syria being liberated, a good number of families, forces changed path from going into Damascus, and they started going to the prisons. Some of you who visited me in the mission will see that I have a picture of a man holding an axe, and hitting a metal steel door trying to open it. That picture resembles what everyone was hoping for to see come out of those prisons— loved ones, mothers, fathers. We saw some. We saw horrific images of children coming out of some of those dungeons and some of those cells. These images will never personally escape me. But on December 8th, The majority of Syrians were celebrating, but the vast majority of them who have loved ones missing were looking, hoping, often with no answer. Not long after that, with this responsibility at hand, we established— the president established by decree the Independent Commission on the Missing and the National— the Transitional Justice Commission, both of whom I'm very humbled to be sharing a panel with here today, Dr. Rada and Salah Abdel-Basat. The 4 of them arrived from Damascus between yesterday and the day before. As you know, this is a big challenge, but they also come here because they feel it is their duty to engage with the international community that stood with them with what they could, as Olivier mentioned, to do what they can here at this forum. They will return with expectations. People are going to ask them, how was New York? What did the international community tell you? What sort of support are you able to offer? What sort of support are the states able to offer? And I know this is not the end of the conversation, but absolutely not even the beginning. The conversation has already started, but a very important milestone to have this ARIA formula here with all of you being present. So my first ask, please, is Listen carefully to what the commissions have to say. Unfortunately, the victims will not be briefing, but they will be around to discuss, to share their experience. But secondly, the least we can do as Syrians— we're very happy to be doing this with Colombia— is to honor people like Yasmin and Safinaz, who came door-knocking here in the United Nations, but also went to the prisons to look for their loved ones. Women across the world put a huge effort and go through incredible stigma and incredible fear of repression, risks, financial risks, personal risks, in order to search for their loved ones. And so before the moratorium kicks in with the beginning of the 81st session, you'll be hearing in written today by us Syria and Colombia, that we wish to honor the women around the world who spend so much effort seeking the truth for their missing persons in a way that is worth remembering them. I look forward to the session today, and I'm very grateful again to the co-sponsors for always standing with Syria and the Syrian people, and I'm so glad that the day has come that all of you are able to see Syria here, co-sponsoring, speaking, but more importantly, national commissions, and most important of all, the families that we're here to talk about. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Ibrahim, Ambassador Arabi, for this important and strong statement, in particular for reminding us the special role of women, unfortunately, around the world in conflict situations and in search of missing persons and their personal sacrifice in this regard. With this, we have been through the sponsors, and I thank again my fellow ambassadors here, the fellow sponsors of this event, and I'll now turn to our panel of distinguished briefers. I'll start to pass the floor to the one person who's not sitting right here, but he should be with us on a video link, Mr. Volker Türk, who is the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Mr. Türk, you have the floor.
There he is.

First of all, thank you very much, and it's a great pleasure to join you by remote from Geneva. And Excellencies, dear co-sponsors, distinguished participants, and I want to acknowledge in particular and honor those who are present in the room who have families who have lost their loved ones or looking for their loved ones. Your fate is the extremely important one for all of us in the United Nations. For much too long, Syria has been associated with conflict, with suffering, and the displacement of millions of its people. But the country's deeper story is one of ancient civilizations, of rich diversity and resilience, and this history and legacy are inseparable from its present and its future. 19 months after the fall of the former regime, following decades of repression, killings, torture, and enforced disappearances, Syrians are feeling a mix of exhaustion, relief, and hope. Their expectations are high on many fronts. They are clamoring for justice, for accountability and transparency. The fractured social contract of the past needs to be rebuilt through trust in state institutions, dealing with the past, healing, and cohesion between communities. This requires meaningful reforms that deliver tangible improvements to people's daily lives. We know from history that transitions are never easy and they don't happen overnight. They require patience and perseverance. And it is clear, and the Ambassador of Syria just mentioned it, the international community has an important role to play. Experience from other countries shows that when transitions fail, it is often because of either inadequate or excessive engagement by international players and insufficient national ownership. Today there is an opportunity to get it right. To do so, we need to focus on Syria's future, and it's clear that human rights are the foundation. It was very much at the foundation of all the ones who struggled for freedom in Syria. The security situation in the country remains fragile, with episodic outbreaks of intercommunal violence in parts of the country. And ongoing Israeli incursions in the south. Economic hardship and delays in restoring basic services are heightening tensions, especially among internally displaced people and those who are returning from abroad. Despite the lifting of some sanctions, the economy is still suffering from their impact over many years, combined with war and displacement. Some 90% of the Syrian population lives below the poverty line. Up to 12 million Syrians have limited access to water and sanitation services. Hate speech is fueling communal tensions and fear, and frustrations are being directed at minority communities. Against this complex background, I am encouraged by positive steps taken by the authorities which can help lay the foundation for a more peaceful future. The government has started to reform institutions and to pursue accountability, including by addressing the fate of missing people. The establishment of the People's Assembly, the constitutional declaration, and security sector reform are important developments. The prosecution of the former president and other officials, while at this stage largely in absentia, is an important step. These proceedings need to respect international standards, and more must follow. Efforts to investigate and prosecute people allegedly responsible for attacks that took place in the coastal areas in March 2025 and in Zweden in July 2025 are also welcome. And the fate— and we have just heard it from all of you— the fate of missing people is a crucial issue. For Syria's future. During my visit to the country in January last year, the first time ever that a High Commissioner for Human Rights visited Syria, I heard again and again from people seeking answers about the fate of their loved ones. Their right to truth is essential for reconciliation and building trust in the state. The National Commission for Transitional Justice and the National Commission for missing persons have a crucial role to play, and they will require sustained political, technical, and financial support. And I look forward to also hearing from not only from them but also from Carla Quintana, who leads the UN support to Syria on missing people. I also welcome greater space for public debate, which is essential to counter hate speech and incitement to violence. And to rebuild social cohesion. The government's efforts to grant citizenship to stateless Kurds, to recognize linguistic diversity, and enable the return of displaced people to their homes are encouraging. The return of some 1.7 million refugees and nearly 2 million internally displaced people to their homes is a welcome sign of growing confidence. Excellencies, it's absolutely key that the transition is fair, inclusive, and responsive to the needs of all Syrians. And I see 4 areas of action where international support can make a difference. First, national ownership, which is a prerequisite for successful transitions. This requires a process that is centered on victims and survivors, including families of the missing, that listens to them, supports them to claim their rights, and addresses their needs. It is crucial to recognize the specific impact of the conflict on women and girls, including sexual violence, discrimination, trauma, and more. It is also important to ensure the meaningful participation of a broad cross-section of society working alongside public institutions, including women, civil society, young people, and affected communities, not outside powers or donor governments. However, well-intentioned. Women-led groups have been the beacon of hope during the horrific years of war and remain so today. And I have met many Syrian women in exile during my years with UNHCR. These women have not only documented violations and demanded justice, they have also offered ideas and solutions for rebuilding society, and their voices need to be heeded. Second, accountability for violations before, during, and since the war is essential regardless of the perpetrator. Steps towards justice need to fully respect international human rights standards, including due process and fair trial guarantees. These efforts need to be part of a comprehensive process that includes effective remedies for victims. The draft transitional justice law is an opportunity to ensure that victims are not left behind, that all crimes are addressed, regardless of when they occurred. And I urge all those with influence to support Syrian efforts towards accountability, which is how institutions earn legitimacy for the future. Third, a successful transition requires meaningful attempts at non-judicial forms of truth-seeking, memorialization, and national reconciliation. Over more than 5 decades of repression, pain, and loss, Syrians have learned better than most what justice, truth, and healing require. That knowledge needs to inform the path ahead. For families of missing people, establishing the truth about what happened to their loved ones is a crucial part of healing. People need spaces where they can speak openly, listen to one another, acknowledge trauma and suffering, and imagine a shared vision for their country. Fourth, people need institutions they can have confidence in. This means strengthening the judicial system, law enforcement, public administration through institutional reform, due process and fair trial guarantees, and torture prevention, all based on international rights standards. United Nations are there to provide support, and the United Nations need to offer a coherent, lean, and effective architecture to back Syria's transitional justice process. We need to approach this work with humility and patience, guided by the ingenuity and dynamism of the Syrian people. During my visit on January 25th, the Syrian leadership assured me of the importance of respecting the human rights of all Syrians, as well as pursuing healing, trust-building, and social cohesion. My office now has a team in Damascus that continues to engage with the authorities. We're providing legal and policy advice on the transitional justice framework, encouraging meaningful consultations with survivors and their families, and supporting economic policies that advance people's rights and improve their lives. For victims, justice is not a nice-to-have. It's fundamental and deeply personal. It's a recognition of their suffering. It's a promise that what happened to them and to their loved ones will not happen again. And we all have a responsibility to uphold that promise and to build and help build a more peaceful and inclusive future for all Syrians. Thank you very much.

I thank Mr. Türk for his briefing, and I now pass the floor to Ms. Carla Quintana, who's Assistant Secretary-General and head of the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic, also known as IIMP. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam President, Madam Chair, Excellencies, dear co-sponsors, colleagues, Dr. Rida Jalhi, Dr. Abdulbaset Abdullatif. to the Syrian families, and especially to the women that are looking for their loved ones. Thank you for convening this timely discussion that places the focus on Syria and the Syrian people and reaffirms the commitment of the UN, as my colleague the High Commissioner just pointed out, and its member states to support them in their quest for a better future. Transitional justice and within it, making the right to truth a reality is an essential component of that quest. Of the many truths that Syria must confront, none is more consequential or more heartrending than the truth about the missing. Disappearance, we are often told, is harder than death. It leaves families suspended between hope and despair. unable to mourn, unable to heal, and unable to move forward. Today, hundreds of thousands remain missing in Syria. Almost every Syrian family has been touched directly or indirectly by this tragedy. Nearly every community continues to live with unanswered questions. Addressing the issue of the missing is, of course, a humanitarian obligation, but it is also indispensable for stabilization, reconciliation and lasting peace. A society cannot rebuild its social fabric while hundreds of thousands of families continue to live without answers. I look forward to updating the General Assembly tomorrow in my annual briefing on the progress that we, at the independent institution, have made in implementing our mandate, in coordination and complementarity with relevant actors. Today, within the broader context of a discussion regarding transitional justice, allow me to share with you 4 key elements that, drawing from comparative experience, I believe are essential to increase the chances of success in the search of the missing: political will, information, trust, and methodology. I am convinced that using these elements as a guide is the best way to monitor progress and to address challenges, both in the search for the missing and more broadly in achieving transitional justice. First, political will is fundamental. Recognizing the existence of a missing persons crisis and the need to establish specialized mechanisms to address it is the first step. This recognition must be accompanied by an adequate legislative and institutional framework, access to information, as well as sufficient funding and resources. Political will creates the opportunity to search. Institutional capacity determines whether that search succeeds. Political will is therefore also required to ensure effective coordination, access to information, openness to international cooperation, and sustained capacity building. Search mechanisms cannot operate in isolation. Political will must extend both internally across national institutions such as the judiciary, forensic services, the police, and civil registry, and externally, of course, through cooperation with relevant international actors backed by sustained political and financial support. It is essential to understand that the search of the missing, as part of the right to the truth, is central to stabilization, sustainable peace, and reconciliation. It must therefore advance alongside progress in justice, reparation, and the prevention of future violations. Second, information. Gathering, analyzing, and sharing information is vital in the search of missing persons. One of the defining features of disappearances is that relevant information is often hidden or dispersed. One of the greatest challenges is piecing together those fragments. Having information adequately flow means that we can provide more and better answers to the families. While technologies enable information to flow more quickly and to analyze it more rapidly, not all the actors possessing information are willing or able, for various reasons, to share it. There is an urgent need to establish systems that enable the secure flow of essential information so as to connect the dots between the various parties involved in the search: national authorities in various countries, international actors, civil society, and the families themselves. Failing or unnecessarily delaying sharing information amounts to misunderstanding the complexity of the search, effectively impeding access to the right to the truth. We have seen this in several countries. Third, trust. The families of the missing are the bastion of dignity and the voice calling for truth and justice. Their trust in the search process is crucial, not only for obtaining information but also for building transparent and participatory processes. Search processes are long. Trust, therefore, is what sustains them. It is through trust that families gain confidence in the process and clarity about what it can and cannot deliver. Trust is built day by day through actions. It cannot be assumed, nor can we expect everyone to trust every institution from the outset. Trust among national institutions and between national and international actors is equally fundamental to building an effective search process. Fourth, methodology. Searching for the missing requires comprehensive processes that have taken us years worldwide to develop. We cannot repeat the same mistakes and expect isolated or fragmented magic formulas to resolve what requires a complex, interdisciplinary, and large-scale process supported by adequate human and material resources. Above all, it requires coordinated efforts. The sooner we begin, the sooner families will receive answers. Needless to say, even when these 4 elements are present, no single institution can implement the search process alone, neither at the national nor at the international level. That is why we always emphasize at the Double IMP that the search for missing persons is a collective process. That requires coordinated and complementary efforts. All relevant actors must have the political will to contribute their fair share. This also requires a legal, political, and technical framework. From a state of total denying of the missing persons crisis until December 2024, Syria has now moved towards establishing such a framework. Comparative experience Such as Colombia, Bosnia, Kuwait, Argentina, Cyprus, Sri Lanka, Iraq, Mexico, Chile, Spain, Morocco, teach us that building the institutional capacity, methodologies, and coordination required to respond to missing persons crises of this magnitude takes time. Those experiences have also taught us that there are no shortcuts and that isolated efforts are not enough no matter how well-intentioned they are. This is precisely why sustained cooperation and coordination, technical support, and openness to hands-on international cooperation and expertise remains so important. I would like to acknowledge the dialogue we have developing— we have been developing with the National Commission of Missing Persons with Dr. Rida Jalhi to start addressing key issues across the full breadth of our respecting mandates. Including harmonizing approaches to case registration, mapping mass graves, strengthening forensic infrastructure, addressing patterns of disappearances, and developing information systems. Many important fundamental questions remain to be answered in Syria, including, for example, regarding the relationship between search and accountability actors and the way their methodologies and findings are connected. The draft law on transitional justice and missing persons can be first important steps to address them within a comprehensive legal, participatory, and political framework. Answering these questions has taken years, decades in other jurisdictions. It requires the engagement of the state as a whole. Drawing on operational experiences from around the world in searching for missing persons and supporting transitional justice processes, The independent institution stands ready to support CIDHIA. We must continue laying the foundation for a process that is reliable, rigorous, sustainable, and nationally led and internationally supported. Clarifying the fate and whereabouts of the missing and fulfilling the right to truth of the families is a key component of transitional justice and an essential precondition to achieve justice peace, stabilization, and reconciliation. Thank you, Madam President.
Shukran.
And I thank ASG Quintana for her briefing. I now pass the floor to Dr. Abdul Latif, Head of the Syrian National Commission on Transitional Justice, to Fatah.

Ladies and gentlemen, Excellencies, at the outset I'd like to thank the organizers of this important meeting, and I express our appreciation for the ongoing efforts of the United Nations and international partners in supporting the Syrian people at this critical stage. I welcome the opportunity to shed light on the issues of transitional justice and missing persons, both of which are among our highest national priorities due to their direct impact on civil peace and confidence-building, and the consolidation of the rule of law. For decades, Syrians have endured grave violations that have left profound scars on society and the state. Today, the transformations taking place in Syria provide a historic opportunity to address this painful legacy in ways that may not have been previously possible. We are driven in this effort by our conviction and determination that transitional justice is not merely about addressing the past, but also about investing in the future. Efforts to uncover the fate of the missing and provide redress for victims and listen to the voices of survivors represent a national and moral commitment that cannot be delayed. The National Commission on Transitional Justice is working on launching a comprehensive process that is based on the principles of truth, accountability, reparations, institutional reform, and guarantees of non-recurrence. And despite the visible progress achieved, we face a group of challenges. The sheer scale of the violations, the complexity of the cases, requires sustained international support that is focused on building national capacity, on transferring expertise, and strengthening Syrian institutions in a manner that preserves the national ownership of this process and enhances the confidence of citizens in it. We affirm our interest in benefiting from the United Nations expertise in the field of transitional justice, of the rule of law, and the protection of victims. We express our appreciation for the role played by the High Commission on Human Rights, as well as the IIMP and the Independent Investigation Committee and the a group of experts, of UN experts on conflict-related sexual violence, and the different United Nations bodies and institutions. We thank them for their contributions in documenting violations, and we believe that we are able to engage into a deeper level of work with the national— between us and them by exchanging expertise and knowledge and capacity building in a manner that would achieve our common goals in uncovering the truth and in preventing non-repetition— in guaranteeing non-repetition, I beg your pardon. The Commission was established by Presidential Decree No. 149 of the 25th of August, 2025. Over almost a year, the Commission has worked on 2 tracks. The first track is an international one that is aimed at learning from contemporary transitional justice experiences around the world and strengthening the relationship between the international community and the United Nations organizations. And within this framework, the Commission signed numerous memoranda of understanding to build capacities and to establish a system for digital security and archives. The Commission has also started drafting a transitional justice law through consultations that were large-scale with various stakeholders, with the victims at the forefront. More than 300 meetings have been held with victims, and the Commission has coordinated with more than 80 civil society organizations. The Commission established 6 departments, each of which has carried out regular visits to Syrian governorates within a strategic approach that was adopted. The Truth Team started case files concerning a number of painful massacres in neighborhoods and towns such as Atadamun, Al-Husayn, and Jalilat al-Fadl and Tasneem in the outskirts of Homs. The Department of Accountability prepares the evidence files and shares them with competent courts. Moreover, investigations are being pursued at multiple locations such as Al-Jura and Al-Qusur in Deir ez-Zor and Daraa and in Damascus and the center of Homs as well. The Department of Operations is setting up the first recovery center in Homs and is working on establishing the National Victims Register, while the Department of Memory is conducting field surveys across Syrian governorates as part of a national memory initiative. The Department of Community Reconciliation continues to organize dialogue among the different segments of Syrian society to ensure civil peace and national reconciliation throughout the Syrian governorates. The Commission also wants to remain close to victims in their own communities and it would like— and it seeks to reduce the burden of travel and guarantee that their voices are heard. Therefore, it will establish branches in all the different governorates. We believe that achieving transitional justice is not only a human rights obligation; rather, it is also a fundamental pillar for consolidating civil peace and preventing the recurrence of conflict. We believe that this contributes directly to enhancing international peace and security— enhancing civil peace and security, and advancing the purposes and principles of the United Nations. Thank you. In this context, we are developing national approaches based on respect for the central roles of victims and survivors and the families of the missing and forcibly disappeared. And we work with civil society and women's organizations in designing programs for truth-seeking, preserving memory, and promoting national reconciliation. We emphasize that transitional justice in Syria will not succeed unless it is Syrian-led and nationally owned and supported by international partnerships that are constructive, and founded on cooperation and mutual respect. Accordingly, we call upon the international community to continue investing in the development of national institutions as an investment in the stability of Syria and the region. We stress that Syrians are not asking the international community to deliver justice on their behalf. Rather, they are asking it to stand by them as they build justice with their own hands in a manner that restores dignity to victims, strengthens confidence in the state, and lays the foundations for sustainable peace. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank Dr. Abdullatif for his briefing, and I now give the floor to Dr. Rida Jalchi, who is Head of the Syrian National Commission on Transitional Justice. You have the floor, sir.

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, the Security Council. Ladies and gentlemen, distinguished members of the Security Council, I have a great honor to address you on behalf of the National Commission for the Missing in the Syrian Arab Republic. And I would like to thank the countries sponsoring this session and all those who have helped keep the issue of missing Syrians present and support their families' rights to know the fate of their loved ones. The issue of the missing is a matter of rights and dignity. sustainable peace. There can be no healing for families without the truth. There can be no stability for society as long as the fate of tens of thousands of its members remains unknown. Following liberation and the fall of the previous regime, the National Commission for the Missing was established in the Syrian Arab Republic to lead efforts to search for the missing and determine their fate, to support families and coordinate related efforts. And within a short period of time, the commission began its practical operations. It determined the fate of a number of missing persons. Most notably the fate of the, the 6 children of Dr. Rania al-Abbasi. It also responded to more than 170 reports of sites suspected to contain graves or human remains. The Commission opened 10 family service centers in all Syrian governorates and launched 11 national programs covering its core areas of work. Madam President, before the fall of the regime, families of missing persons, Syrian civil society organizations, and a number of countries and international organizations made significant efforts to document cases and to advocate for the rights of the families. Syria's stability is also key to achieving a lasting peace across the entire region. Spain is committed to the political transition process in Syria, and we recognize the work of Syrian authorities through the National Commission on Transitional Justice and the National Commission on Missing Persons. It's important that both commissions operate under the highest international standards, guaranteeing their full independence and impartiality and their cooperation with the United Nations. Support for the victims is a priority of Spain's foreign policy. We believe that it is vitally important to ensure the effective involvement of victims and civil society in the transitional justice process in Syria. The families of missing persons have played a fundamental role in the quest for truth, in the preservation of memory, and in promoting reconciliation. The participation of Syrian women's associations is also crucial— this in line with the Women, Peace and Security Agenda. Their full, equal, and effective participation in all decision-making processes in Syria will ensure the success of the transition that has been launched. Spain will continue to support Syrian institutions and the Syrian people to advance in this direction. Chairman, we stand at a crucial time for Syria and its people in which, together with the challenge of rebuilding and consolidating legitimate institutions and democratic institutions after a decade of conflict, there are worrisome internal and external pressures, a profound humanitarian crisis, millions of displaced and refugees, security challenges in light of the current regional geopolitical situation. Syria will only be able to overcome these challenges if we are able to guarantee the full respect for its sovereignty, sovereign independence, and territorial integrity. The international community must support these Syrian efforts by respecting national leadership, fully promoting universality indivisibility, and independence of all human rights, the rule of law, and the fight against impunity. In this context, Spain steadfastly supports national and international efforts to ensure accountability and combat impunity in Syria. We highlight the work of the international mechanism— the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism for Syria established by the UN General Assembly, which we support through regular financial contributions. We encourage other countries to support the mechanism and international and national efforts to support accountability processes in Syria. Finally, and to conclude, Spain will continue to defend transitional justice as an essential component to ensure that Syria can move towards a peaceful, inclusive political process guaranteeing the fundamental rights of all citizens without any form of discrimination, in strict compliance with international human rights and humanitarian law.

Thank you.

This is a commitment through which Syria can count on the full support of Spain. Thank you very much.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Spain for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Japan.

I thank you, Mr. President. I thank the organizer and co-sponsors for convening this. Thank you, Mr. President, for hosting this meeting, and I thank the briefers for their valuable insights. Since the fall of the former authority, the situation both within and outside Syria has undergone dramatic changes. Japan is committed to providing concrete support for an inclusive, peaceful, and stable transition led by the Syrian government and its people, both bilaterally and in coordination with the international community. We welcome the progress made— being made in the political transition process, including last week's inaugural session of the People's Assembly. At the same time, numerous challenges remain, including domestic security issues and economic recovery. And these challenges must be addressed effectively to gain strong support from Syrians as well as the international community. Japan firmly supports the work of the Independent Institution of Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic for their role in supporting Syrian-led and Syrian-owned efforts to clarify the fate and whereabouts of all missing persons and provide support to their families. This is not only a humanitarian imperative, but contributes to national reconciliation and transitional justice, fostering social cohesion and restoring dignity to victims. Japan welcomes the IIMP's continued collaboration with the Syrian authorities, including the National Commission on Missing Persons, and the development of their joint work plan last December. We also commend its growing cooperation with international stakeholders, including the ICRC, family associations, and civil society organizations toward effective implementation of its mandate. Mr. President, Japan stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors, and families of missing persons in Syria. We remain committed to supporting efforts to uncover the truth, advance justice, and support a Syrian-led transition to a lasting peace. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Japan for your statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Estonia.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Estonia aligns itself with the statement of the European Union and the statement of the Global Alliance for the Missing. We thank Colombia, Denmark, Luxembourg, and Syria for organizing the meeting, and the preface for their invaluable insights. For decades, the Syrian people have suffered systematic repression, enforced disappearances, unlawful killings, arbitrary detentions, and other violations. Despite the fall of the Assad regime, hundreds of thousands of Syrians continue to live in uncertainty about the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones. Their suffering is not over before they know the truth. The search for missing persons is therefore urgent. Estonia commends the work of all entities that work— that are working tirelessly to find answers to the families and close ones of thousands of missing persons. We strongly support the Syrian-led and Syrian-owned process led by the National Commission for Missing Persons. We emphasize that this is a collective undertaking. Strong cooperation with international actors, including the Independent Institution of Missing Persons, the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism, and the Commission of Inquiry accelerates the progress towards the shared goal. Clarifying the fates and whereabouts of missing persons is a humanitarian imperative. Estonia supports— Estonia's support to Syrian humanitarian crisis has been more than €12.6 million since 2011. We have funded the activities of ICRC, UNICEF, UNHCR, OCHA, IOM, and WFP. In addition, Estonia's NGOs are improving the education and livelihoods of IDPs and Syrian refugees in neighboring countries, including helping to develop young people's digital skills. Estonia remains steadfast in its commitment to international humanitarian law, and we welcome Syria's entry to the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law. While the mandate is humanitarian in nature, the impact of establishing the truth reaches far beyond humanitarian sphere. It is an essential element of transitional justice, which in turn is a key component of national reconciliation and lasting peace. For transitional justice, it is equally important to guarantee non-recurrence and address accountability. While significant challenges persist, Syria has demonstrated its commitment to address them, and the international community must maintain its support to ensure that their endeavour succeeds. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Estonia for her statement, and now I give the floor to the last speaker inscribed on the speakers' list, the representative of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of the Benelux countries, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands, we would like to thank the organizing member states and the briefers for today's session. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by the European Union. More than a decade of conflict has left hundreds of thousands of Syrians searching for answers about the fate and whereabouts of living— of missing loved ones. Behind every statistic is a family living with uncertainty, grief, and the painful absence of closure. The Benelux countries remain firmly committed to a Syrian-led, victim-centered, and rights-based transitional justice process. Transitional justice constitutes a fundamental pillar of any serious path toward building sustainable peace and stability. Any delay in advancing transitional justice does not only jeopardize the future but poses serious challenges today. We would like to highlight 3 points. First, strong complementarity between national institutions and international actors is vital. We encourage structured cooperation between the Syrian National Commissions on Transitional Justice and on Missing Persons with the IIMP, the IIIM, and the Commission of Inquiry, with robust safeguards for victims' consent, data protection, and evidence preservation. Second, transitional justice must address violations of all parties, past and present. Any legal framework that limits accountability to crimes of a single period or actor risks undermining victims' trust, entrenching impunity, and sowing the seeds of future violence. Third, we encourage the Syrian government to pursue its efforts and build national ownership. The national commissions should clearly communicate their work to the public and meaningfully engage victims and civil society. The full, equal, and meaningful participation of women throughout the process must be ensured. The Benelux countries will continue to support international accountability, transitional justice, and efforts to clarify the fate and whereabouts of all missing persons in Syria and support their families. Thank you.

I thank the representative of the Netherlands. Colleagues, this brings us to the end of this session. If you allow me, I'll just deliver very quick closing remarks. I'll also be making 3 points. On the way into this session— and that's going to be my first— I told my colleagues here while I was briefing them that they're going to come into a room friends. Thank you for proving me right. Finally, this issue is a matter of consensus, a matter where there is national ownership, where there's national effort, international support from the Secretariat and the organizations, and from the member states. My second point is that you have heard of the efforts that my colleagues are doing on the ground. The Commission being here, the victims and the survivors and their families coming all the way from Syria to be here with us today is not something that is easy. But it shows that our efforts are real. It shows that your efforts are real. Here in New York, there is a lot that we can do. You have proven that you can stand with the Syrian people in the past, and now, where the situation has allowed itself further and further, it's time to prove that we can do that again, together, with national ownership, as you have said. My final point is that, as a reminder, that Colombia and Syria are putting together an initiative to present a text to the GA before the 81st session. starts. We'll be circulating a letter later to this effect that shows what, what the effort is and why we're doing it. Today, this or that effort is about Syrian women, Colombian women, and women from all across the world who have worked so hard to reveal the fate of the missing. Some of them are with us here today, but I hope that the effort that Colombia and Syria will be leading on with your support is something that we can do to honor all women across the world who have worked tirelessly to uncover the missing. Finally, I would really like to thank the Permanent Representatives, the Ambassadors, the Deputy Ambassadors who have been with us, some throughout the whole event, some who managed through their tight schedule to come and to present. So please, to the experts with us in the room, do please thank them for us personally, but thank you to all the experts in the room for what I know helps in preparing briefing remarks and positions and discussing with capitals. This event for us is not just a, you know, I was just going to say not a one-off, but it is an event that really is meaningful because I have colleagues from Damascus who have heard supporting statements while they confront some of the most horrific legacies. I get to work also on things that are hopeful and optimistic, but my colleagues who work on the missing, who work on transitional justice, have to confront the crimes of the last 14 years and the last 60 years. every single day, and they can come here calm and collected to present how they would like to do this together with you, the international community. Thank you again. Please stay safe. It seems a bit stormy outside judging by some of the raincoats that came in, and I look forward to what we can do together. Thank you.
